raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old female who was diagnosed with HIV infection in 2010 and lost follow-up for almost five years presented to our hospital on March 31, 2015, with acquired immunodeficiency virus syndrome (AIDS), which defines illnesses including wasting syndrome. Her vitals were as follows: weight: 25 kg, height: 155 cm, body mass index (BMI): 10.4 kg/m2), Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) (hypoxemia and bilateral interstitial pulmonary infiltrates), chronic diarrhea secondary to cryptosporidiosis, severe oral candidiasis and chronic herpetic oral ulcers, pancytopenia, and cholestatic jaundice (total bilirubin: 84 umol/L, direct bilirubin: 72 umol/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP): 1400 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT): 581 U/L, aspartate transferase (AST): 149 U/L, alanine transferase (ALT): 82 U/L, and renal glucose urea: 2.3 mmol/L). Abdominal ultrasound showed biliary sludge with no intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilation, while magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed an enlarged (21 cm diameter) fatty liver with mild dilatation of the intra- and extrahepatic biliary systems and multiple areas of narrowing and stricture formation with no obvious intrahepatic stone formation (Figure 1).
A liver biopsy showed chronic inflammation, a single granuloma with mild fibrosis, marked steatosis, and no evidence of malignancy. Cholangiopathy secondary to HIV or cryptosporidium with concomitant hepatic typical (tuberculosis) or atypical (Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare infection (MAI)) infection was diagnosed. The laboratory investigations revealed an HIV viral load of 2,566,506 copies/ml and a CD4 count nadir of 12 cells/mm3. Moreover, genotypic resistance testing revealed no significant resistance-conferring mutations. The patient was treated for her presumed hepatic tuberculosis or MAI infection with first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) along with clarithromycin for MAI. She also received full treatment for PCP with cotrimoxazole and prednisone for 21 days, followed by secondary prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole, and was commenced on TDF/emtricitabine (co-formulated as Truvada ) and efavirenz on April 5, 2015. Twenty-one days after the initiation of TDF, the previously normal serum potassium (4.7 mmol/L) and phosphate (0.81 mmol/L) levels were noticed to be low (potassium: 2.8 mmol/L, phosphate: 0.36 mmol/L) with a normal magnesium level (1.11 mmol/L). Since the patient had severe anemia (hemoglobin: 5.9 g/dL) that precluded the use of zidovudine as an alternative to TDF and the unavailability of abacavir, the TDF was continued as the benefit of treating the patient's advanced HIV infection outweighed the adverse effect of TDF-induced tubulopathy. However, when the patient's hemoglobin improved to 9.4 g/dL, TDF/emtricitabine (Truvada ) was changed to zidovudine/lamivudine on February 10, 2016, because of persistent hypokalemia.
In April 2016, zidovudine/lamivudine was changed back to TDF/emtricitabine because of worsening anemia induced by zidovudine (hemoglobin dropped from 9.4 to 6.9 g/dL). However, in May 2016 (13 months after initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART)), the patient's investigations were remarkable for persistent hypokalemia (2.6 mmol/L) and hypophosphatemia (0.66 mmol/L), undetectable HIV viral load, a CD4 count of 292 cells/uL, and hemoglobin of 9.7 g/dL. Due to concerns about TDF-induced tubulopathy and the improvement of her hemoglobin level, her antiretroviral regimen was changed to zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz. However, this regimen was stopped in December 2016 due to acute pancreatitis (amylase: 2620 U/L (N: 25-115) and lipase: 8015 u/L (N: 73-393)) thought to be caused by at least one of its components (TDF, emtricitabine, or efavirenz). A month later, her HIV viral load rose to 4,282,432 copies/mL, and her CD4 count dropped to 85 cells/uL. The HAART regimen was planned to be resumed after recovery from acute pancreatitis, but the patient was lost to follow-up for almost a year.
In June 2018, the patient presented again for follow-up. Her HIV viral load was 2,473,928 copies/mL, and her CD4 count was 83 cells/uL. Repeated genotypic resistance testing revealed no resistance to any nucleotide/nucleoside or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors or protease inhibitors. As a result, she was commenced on elvitegravir 150 mg, cobicistat 150 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, and tenofovir alafenamide 10 mg co-formulated tables (Genvoya). However, when seen in a follow-up 14 months later, in August 2019, the patient's viral load was not completely suppressed (1,840 copies/mL), and the CD4 count was 169 cells/uL. The patient admitted to being non-adherent to therapy. At that time, the patient complained of a dull ache in the back, generalized bone pain, and myalgia. On examination, she was cachectic (weight: 36 kg, height: 155 cm, BMI: 15 kg/m2), had a waddling gait with tender points at the thoracolumbar region of the spine, and had severe proximal myopathy. An MRI of the spine confirmed the presence of compression fractures of the 12th-thoracic and first-lumbar vertebrae (T12-L1) and her bone densitometry revealed a Z-score of -6.4 at the lumbar spine and -5 at the femoral neck (Figure 2).
She was subsequently investigated for the causes of low bone mass. There was evidence of low vitamin D levels, which can be attributed to a lack of sun exposure along with impaired hepatic function and the expected dysfunctional hydroxylation of vitamin D at position 25. In addition, there was a chronic state of phosphate wasting that was not treated even after stopping TDF and switching to TAF. Her laboratory work-up excluded other causes of low bone mass at a young age, such as primary hyperparathyroidism, hypogonadism, thyrotoxicosis, renal failure, and medications. Detailed investigations are presented in Table 1.
Accordingly, the diagnosis of TDF-related Fanconi syndrome was made based on serum bone minerals (Table 1) and urine parameters as shown in Table 2.
She was treated for her pathological fracture conservatively with active vitamin D replacement along with calcium. The patient was also treated with combined estrogen/progesterone replacement, as she had been amenorrheic for seven months. This hormonal therapy was planned to be given until the patient reached her normal age of menopause.
At the follow-up visit three months later, the patient reported remarkable improvement in her muscle and back pain. Her gait was steadier, and her muscle strength was better. She continued on vitamin D, calcium, and estrogen/progesterone combinations, with no further fractures reported during her follow-up period. Unfortunately, the patient passed away in July 2020 due to severe COVID-19 pneumonia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old female with untreated HIV infection presented on March 31, 2015 with severe wasting, dyspnea, chronic diarrhea, painful oral ulcers, and jaundice, and later presented in August 2019 with chronic back pain, generalized bone pain, and myalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV in 2010 and lost to follow-up for nearly 5 years, she presented in March 2015 with profound wasting, hypoxemic pneumonia, cryptosporidial diarrhea, oral thrush, herpetic oral ulcers, and cholestatic jaundice. Following initiation of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)/emtricitabine and efavirenz in April 2015, she developed persistent hypokalemia and hypophosphatemia within 21 days, recurrent zidovudine-induced anemia when switched, acute pancreatitis in December 2016 prompting treatment interruption, and subsequent loss to follow-up until June 2018 when she was started on elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Genvoya). In August 2019, she presented with dull thoracolumbar back pain, generalized bone pain, myalgias, proximal muscle weakness, and 7 months of secondary amenorrhea.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in 2010 with 5-year loss to follow-up; AIDS-defining wasting syndrome, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, chronic intestinal cryptosporidiosis, oral candidiasis, chronic oral herpes simplex ulcers, HIV/cryptosporidial cholangiopathy with granulomatous hepatitis, drug-induced acute pancreatitis (December 2016), and secondary amenorrhea.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive initially for profound weight loss, dyspnea, chronic diarrhea, oral thrush/ulcers, and jaundice; positive in August 2019 for back ache, generalized bone pain, myalgia, gait difficulty, and 7-month amenorrhea. Home medication in 2019: elvitegravir 150 mg / cobicistat 150 mg / emtricitabine 200 mg / tenofovir alafenamide 10 mg (Genvoya) with partial non-adherence.

objective.physical_examination: Initial March 2015 exam: profound cachexia (weight 25 kg, height 155 cm, BMI 10.4 kg/m2), hypoxemia, jaundice, severe oral candidiasis, and chronic herpetic oral ulcers. August 2019 exam: cachectic appearance (weight 36 kg, height 155 cm, BMI 15 kg/m2), waddling gait, thoracolumbar spinal tenderness, and severe proximal myopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: March 2015 baseline labs: pancytopenia (hemoglobin 5.9 g/dL), total bilirubin 84 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 72 µmol/L, ALP 1,400 U/L, GGT 581 U/L, AST 149 U/L, ALT 82 U/L, urea 2.3 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, and phosphate 0.81 mmol/L. At day 21 of TDF therapy: hypokalemia (2.8 mmol/L) and hypophosphatemia (0.36 mmol/L) with normal magnesium (1.11 mmol/L); May 2016 labs showed potassium 2.6 mmol/L, phosphate 0.66 mmol/L, and hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL; December 2016 pancreatitis flare showed amylase 2,620 U/L (normal 25–115) and lipase 8,015 U/L (normal 73–393). Abdominal ultrasound (2015) showed biliary sludge without ductal dilation. Workup in 2019 demonstrated low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, persistent urinary phosphate wasting and renal tubular abnormalities, and excluded primary hyperparathyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, and renal failure.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 12 cells/mm3 at baseline (March 2015), rose to 292 cells/µL in May 2016, fell to 85 cells/µL in January 2017 and 83 cells/µL in June 2018, and was 169 cells/µL in August 2019. MRCP (2015) showed hepatomegaly (21 cm fatty liver) with mild intra- and extrahepatic biliary dilation and multifocal strictures without stones. Liver biopsy (2015) showed chronic inflammation, a single granuloma, mild fibrosis, and marked steatosis without malignancy. Spine MRI (August 2019) confirmed T12 and L1 vertebral compression fractures, and DXA bone densitometry showed severe osteoporosis/osteomalacia (Z-score -6.4 at lumbar spine, -5.0 at femoral neck).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Advanced HIV/AIDS (baseline HIV-1 viral load 2,566,506 copies/mL and CD4 count 12 cells/mm3; wild-type on HIV genotypic resistance testing in 2015 and 2018; viral load 1,840 copies/mL in August 2019 on Genvoya) complicated by tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)-induced Fanconi syndrome (proximal renal tubular acidosis, persistent hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and osteomalacia) resulting in pathological T12–L1 vertebral compression fractures, alongside prior Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, cryptosporidiosis, and AIDS cholangiopathy/granulomatous hepatitis. Initial opportunistic infections were treated with cotrimoxazole and prednisone (21 days, then cotrimoxazole prophylaxis) plus isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and clarithromycin. Following transition to elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Genvoya), the T12–L1 fractures and Fanconi osteomalacia were managed conservatively with active vitamin D, calcium supplementation, and combined estrogen/progesterone replacement therapy, leading to marked improvement in back/muscle pain, proximal strength, and gait stability at 3 months without new fractures; the patient later died in July 2020 from severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
